Divided Fates #1

Să închizi o pasăre sălbatică

Brooke Fast, Liviu Szoke (Translator)

3.94
38,466 ratings8,865 reviews
Rate this book
Să închizi o pasăre sălbatică este o poveste de dragoste distopică, perfectă pentru fanii Divergent şi Prison Break, oferind elemente de forced proximity şi un ritm alert, care te va ţine cu sufletul la gură.

Pășește în lumea brutală din Endlock, o închisoare unde cei bogați îi vânează de plăcere pe deținuți!

În oraşul Dividium, legea este simplă: comite o infracţiune, iar pedeapsa este închisoarea pe viaţă la Endlock.

Raven Thorne este cea mai faimoasă figură printre vânătorii de recompense din Dividium. Trăind la marginea societăţii, tânăra nu se dă în lături de la nimic, însă când fratele ei mai mic, Jed, este condamnat la Endlock, Raven va face orice pentru a-l salva – chiar dacă asta înseamnă să se lase arestată.

Acum, captivă într-o închisoare unde pericolul pândeşte la tot pasul, Raven trebuie să-şi folosească toată viclenia şi forţa pentru a-l proteja pe Jed – şi pe ea însăşi, dacă vrea să îşi ducă la bun sfârşit misiunea periculoasă. Dar există un obstacol la care nu s-a aşteptat niciodată: gardianul care trezeşte ceva adânc în interiorul ei. Omul pe care ar trebui să-l urască. Omul ale cărui motive reale par imposibil de descifrat.

Într-o lume în care încrederea este o armă, iar iubirea te face vulnerabil, Raven trebuie să hotărască dacă va risca totul pentru a dărâma un sistem corupt.



„O poveste de dragoste palpitantă, plină de acţiune, perfectă pentru fanii seriei JOCURILE FOAMEI. N-am putut să las cartea din mână!” MELISSA LANDERS, autoare de bestsellere New York Times

„Am devorat Să închizi o pasăre sălbatică! Este captivantă, emoţionantă, un pic prea actuală pentru a fi confortabilă şi imposibil de lăsat din mână. Iar faptul că acesta este debutul lui Brooke Fast? Incredibil! Un prim roman remarcabil! About the author

Brooke Fast

6 books810 followers
Brooke Fast is a lover of dystopian, fantasy, and all things romance. When she’s not writing new worlds, you can find her curled up on the couch with her husband and their pups in their self-built tiny house in the mountains of Maine. She’ll either be consuming copious amounts of coffee and thumbing through the latest romantasy release or sharing book reviews and writing snippets under her alter-ego, @librarybrookes. SK
688 reviews13.8k followers
March 22, 2026
So disappointed in this one. It had such an amazing idea and the plot has substance to it. But the execution? Poor and deeply flawed imo.

From the start it is fast paced. And I won't say this is a good thing now that I'm done with the book. It gives no space for the reader to grasp the severity of the situation the author is trying to show us. Like let me breathe with the characters!! Let me feel the importance of the moment. Give me tension that brews and sits for longer than a few pages!!

Then we have the world building. It's got potential, I think it could have built onto something more cleaner. The execution didn't do it justice. It also makes me link it to the lack of high stakes. There's no ripple effect. There's no situation that makes me feel that "oh damn the stakes are much more higher than I thought." And that instantly shatters the levels of my investment.

Coming to my next complaint. The fmc Raven. She has no emotions apart from her brother Jed. No, I don't consider what she has with Vale as emotional. And I'll elaborate on it further. But Raven, she reads so clinical. I can't relate to her or understand her. Sure she has that lethal reputation and a brother. And that's pretty much her entire personality from other's perspective. But she doesn't open up. We're not shown enough of her processing intense situations. She is robotic to me.

There was a moment when she is zapped and the shock is so intense she says to Vale to unalive him. Now, where is the build up for that statement?? When he had to zap her... Where is the tension?? Why are you not making me sweat with them in concern?? Why is it easily brushed off in two lines?? Then Vale actually shows concern (thank god for that) and she shrugs, focusing more on flirtations and sarcasm. There's no vulnerability that comes across genuine!!

As for the romance? Nope, not a fan. Insta lovey. Vale has known her like a day. And you want me to believe that the guard is now a protector and calls her "little bird" instantly? Hell no. There's lack of chemistry. The tension is only there because of their circumstances rather than their connection. Tbh? Do they actually get into the prisoner x prison guard dynamic? Imo no!! Because it comes across as prisoner x protector the whole time!!!

I didn't care about the ending and it's unlikely I'll continue this series. The only reason I give it two stars is because of world building potential and that the found family kept my interest enough to finish it. Other than that, yeah no. This read more like a YA book with a poor editor.


~•~•~

2.5 ★— 2025 seems to be shaping up as a tentative return for dystopian romances, and To Cage a Wild Bird is very much a throwback to the fast-paced, action-filled YA titles that dominated the 2010s.

The story is set in Dividium, a very on-the-nose name for the war-torn, decimated world where the plot unfolds. Unfortunately, that same genericness carries over into nearly every other aspect of the book.

Our heroine, Raven Thorne, is your classic cookie-cutter early-twenties main character just trying to keep her younger brother safe while surviving as part of the vulnerable underclass of her world, forced to walk on eggshells to stay alive. When her brother is taken to Endlock Prison, she jumps into action, allying with a rebel group who promise to help rescue him, but only if she goes undercover as a prisoner herself to free one of their own.

Raven is the typical protagonist of this genre. She’s brave, hardened, and smart, which are all the usual traits you’d expect her to have. The only truly interesting angle is her backstory as a bounty hunter who captured criminals for money. That could have been such a fascinating internal dilemma, especially once she’s thrown into Endlock alongside people she has personally put there.

But the book barely explores this beyond a couple of scenes, which felt like a true missed opportunity for more interesting conflict. Instead, Raven’s time in prison and the whole undercover mission feel just as underwhelming and predictable as the book overall.

The prison setting itself had potential. There’s a ranking system for prisoners, and the wealthy pay to hunt the highly ranked ones. The more hunts you survive, the higher your rank and the more danger you’re in. It’s a genuinely cool concept! Yet all this is treated so shallowly that I kept wondering how such a cool world-building idea could have been executed in such a lackluster manner.

The romance just continued in bolstering this feeling. Raven’s relationship with the guard MMC, Vale, has zero build-up. I wouldn’t call it slow burn at all, because it’s basically insta-love. They meet once, and by their third scene together, he’s suddenly calling her “little bird” and acting protective, and then boom, they’re in love.

Vale himself is barely a character. Beyond a few scraps of backstory, there’s nothing to him. No personality, no depth. Honestly, I found myself wishing Raven would end up with August, a character who was far more fleshed out and had many more interactions with her.

In the end, I’d sum this book up as predictable, slightly trashy comfort food. It might work if you’re craving some smutty, 2010s-style dystopian nostalgia with a bit of action thrown in. But don’t expect anything groundbreaking.

🎧Audiobook Note
🎙️Narration Style: Solo
The narrator did a great job emoting and giving distinct voices to the characters. I didn’t love the raspy tone she used for Vale, but otherwise, her cadence was soothing and pleasant, making for a very enjoyable listening experience.

I’m a die hard dystopian/apocalyptic fan and I love that it’s making a comeback. This is a mixed bag of Prison Break and Hunger Games but in a prison setting where the rich pay to hunt the prisoners. A bounty hunter gets herself deliberately imprisoned to Endlock in order to save her younger brother. Once there, she makes a ton of enemies but also allies and catches the eyes of a guard who challenges everything that she believes in. Her survival becomes a deadly game of battle, trust and sacrifice.

While I did enjoy it, it had a very flat storyline with minimal character development (we don’t know much about any of them, just the superficial details). It didn’t carry the tempo I was expecting from a dystopian genre but it also read like a YA novel in my opinion. Insta-lusty, built on almost nothing, romance was a miss for me here. I didn’t understand it, it just happened, you just have to go along with it to enjoy the book.

Full RTF!

When I saw someone describe this as The Hunger Games meets Prison Break and Squid Game, I was sold. Dystopian stories are one of my favorite kinds of reads, so this already had a strong chance of working for me.

What to Expect:
➼ Slow Burn
➼ Forbidden Romance
➼ Bounty Hunter FMC
➼ Prisoner x Guard
➼ Prisoners Hunted for Sport
➼ Found Family
➼ Who did this to you?
➼ Dystopian Romance
➼ Narrated by Nikki Massoud
➼ First Person Single POV

I really enjoyed this one! I’ve seen people describe this as Hunger Games in a prison setting but that’s not quite right. It definitely has a similar vibe, but there’s no competition between the inmates. Some of them hate each other, sure, but they could all technically make it out alive.

Instead of a deadly competition, they are hunted for sport by wealthy citizens who essentially pay for the opportunity to murder them. Because they’re “criminals,” their society no longer feels any remorse for killing them. I really miss the days when books like this felt like complete fiction. Now I’m like, “don’t give them ideas!” In the U.S., I think we’re already well on our way to dehumanizing entire groups of people to a point where this plot unfortunately doesn’t even feel that far removed from reality.

This was a pretty straight forward and predictable plot, but I thought it was well written and the author did a great job developing the relationships between the characters. I really enjoyed the relationship progression between the two MC’s but I also thought she did a great job cultivating the found family dynamics and developing the side characters as well.

I don’t want to give too many details, but the ending laid a great foundation for book two! I’m expecting there to be a lot of new characters added to the story and I think they’ll really be able to start fighting back which should make for a very interesting sequel! There were also new dangers introduced for some of the characters that I think will add another layer and keep the next portion of the story from feeling too reminiscent of book one. All in all a very promising start to the series! Looking forward to continuing this one!

ੈ✩‧₊˚ my thoughts

Dystopia is so back.

“I suppose anyone foolish enough to cage a wild bird shouldn’t expect them to sing for their captor.”


To Cage a Wild Bird was messy, emotional, addictive, and honestly hard to put down. Brooke Fast delivers a dystopian romance that leans fully into obsession, control, vulnerability, and complicated characters who make terrible decisions but somehow keep you invested anyway.

The chemistry between Vale and Raven was intense from the start, and the tension carried the story really well. I especially liked how raw the emotional moments felt; there’s pain, longing, and just enough softness hidden beneath all the chaos to make you root for them.

That said, some parts felt a little drawn out, and I wanted a bit more depth or development in certain scenes and character motivations. One of my min criticisms would be that the tension between Vale and Raven could have been more drawn out if certain writing decisions weren’t made. But still, I enjoyed the budding relationship between them and other characters

Still, if you enjoy dystopian romance with high emotional stakes, true devotion, and characters who are equal parts fascinating and infuriating, this one is worth picking up. Not perfect, but definitely memorable.

This was a quick fun read. The audiobook narrator really added to my overall enjoyment of the book. She is one of my favorites and did a fantastic job. I don’t think I would have enjoyed this quite as much via print.

The shock factor and the corruption are strong here, you definitely feel bad for the inmates and the lower classes but it lacked in overall world-building. We’re not given enough information on how the world got to where it is, how the government functions, what the rebellion is even trying to accomplish. Granted this is the first book in the series but I still wanted more.

The romance was fine, a bit cheesy at times but still enjoyable enough to read. Definitely a forbidden romance, NOT enemies-to-lovers.

Overall this was a good time, not a great time. A bit predictable, not quite as developed as I would have liked but worth a listen on audio if the synopsis appeals to you.

I will read the next book in the series, especially if the audiobook is narrated by Nikki Massoud.

📚 For fans of Powerless and Silver Elite (low world-building, high romance).
Although I highly recommend reading ⛓️Chain Gang Allstars by Nana Kwame Adjei-Brenyah⛓️ if you want a true dystopian world set in a Hunger Games style prison that actually feels adult.

There are already many gushing reviews, so rather than repeating the very few parts that were entertaining in this quick read (due to the simple prose), I will focus on what didn't work for me:

- Aside from the 2.5 mediocre spicy scenes, this reads as YA, not adult. The characters could be teenagers due to the way they interact with and consider their dystopian world on a superficial level.

- The dystopian themes are also explored in the same surface level way. Unfortunately, there is nothing new or unique about this dystopian backdrop. It feels very vague and made fit for purpose, rather than created holistically and explored in a way that would have produced a more immersive setting and a less predictable plot. The story did not feel intrinsically linked to the city. It could have been set in any country at any time and still felt the same.

- Within a few lines of meeting, the two main characters are making out. There's no enemy to lovers or slow burn. They insta fall hard and fast, and the rest of the book is just them sneaking around and helping each other while trying not to get caught. This is why I say it's far more teenage than adult. Adults would have battled against their internal morals and questioned each others allegiances way more. This was all done superficially and quick.

- Similarly, the character development across the board was poor, either no one changed, or when they did it was an all at once change done cringe-ly to serve the plot. The friendships with multiple other characters felt rushed and unearned. Hence when a side character gets hurt or worse, we don't really feel much and the scene doesn't hit as hard as it's supposed to.

- The plot and ending is 1:1 exactly what you think it's going to be if you've read or watched any early 2000's dystopia. I'm disappointed nothing new was brought to the table. Nothing was challenged. I completely see how if this is your first Dystopia book then it's new and exciting, but for seasoned readers, this is as disappointing as Silver Elite, a predictable, watered down "dystopia" with nothing new to mull over.

- If a group of motley teens are going to take down an entire government established regime, writers need to prove what it is that makes this group so much better, than the already equipped and solidified resistance that has been trying to do the same thing for years.

One star because I like the author and one star because I respect the arduous work of writing a complete book.

Again, if you want a thorough, unpredictable, well developed, emotional and moving dystopia set in a Prison with Hunger Games style games, then I recommend reading Chain Gang Allstars by Nana Kwame Adjei-Brenyah.
To Cage a Wild Bird does not have the poignant dystopian criticism you would expect of an adult novel and I wouldn't compare it to the Hunger Games which does dystopian criticism in a much more engaging manner.

Thank you so much to Avon Books for providing me with an ARC in exchange for an honest review!

I need white authors to stop writing dystopian novels simply because they like the aesthetic thank you!

*sigh* Where do I begin with this book?

First off, this book is written by someone who was a bookstagrammer, and I was already a little apprehensive of it because of that. (I quite frankly think there are very few book creators in this space who are also excellent writers.) So, I had low expectations because of this reason.

I also had low expectations about this book because the author and publisher have been marketing it as a dystopian romance by both the author and the publisher. I was apprehensive about this because "dystopian romance" tells me that authors want to write an action romance book with smut with a dystopian aesthetic, not an actual dystopian romance.

However, I then saw a couple of interview clips with the author of To Cage a Wild Bird talking about her book. In these interview clips, she talks about how the private, for-profit prison industrial complex is what inspired her to write To Cage a Wild Bird. She talked about it so seriously in this interview, that I thought she would take this book and the dystopian genre seriously. Because in my opinion, that’s what you have to do if you’re writing dystopian.

The very nature of the dystopian genre is to be critiquing the world that you’re living in or that you will be living in the near future. (And god knows that we are living in a dystopian hellscape today.) Dystopian books are usually set in the near future to generate urgency about real current events. They're supposed to speculate what might happen to society if humans don’t deal with existential threats like climate change, oppression, genocide, epidemics, etc.. It’s not a world you’re supposed to fantasize about living in--in fact, it’s supposed to be the opposite. And if you’re writing scenes where the main characters are falling in love with their oppressors, fantasizing about being in a forbidden romance with their oppressors, romanticizing this environment they’re in, when there are so many people in this world that are suffering at the hands of their oppressors and how our world is built and set up and governed today, you are so ignorant and have such a severe level of dissonance that I need you to do some self-reflecting. And you know that it is only white authors who are doing this, because they’ve never experienced any form of violent oppression in their lives.

Even beyond these issues, there were also so many worldbuilding issues. This book is riddled with convenient loopholes that the author wrote in to make the plot advance easier. The book is set in a prison, but there are so many convenient rules built in. I'm the last person to defend prison systems, but in what world are prisoners allowed to freely walk from cell to cell, when the prison they're in is supposedly the most advanced, high-security prison that exists in this world? How do guards not realize that one of their low-level guards constantly disappears or gives preferential treatments to the same inmates over and over again? It doesn't make any sense!

Anyway, if you can’t tell, I didn’t enjoy this. I think I’m officially taking a break from reading any dystopian book written by a white author to preserve my sanity.

3.5 stars

I think if I had read this ten years ago, I would have enjoyed it a lot more. It reminded me a lot of older dystopian. However I will admit, as an adult, I haven't had much luck enjoying the genre. This book is a debut and I think that shows in the writing. This is being marketed for an adult audience and it reads a lot more like YA (spice excluded). Fast tends to overuse a lot of phrases as well. Please do not take a shot every time she says "his eyes darkened" because I am pretty sure you would pass out. I didn't dislike the characters but also didn't feel very connected to them either.

I was initially annoyed at how easy it was for anyone to be arrested and sent to a prison that would lead to certain death. You can get sent there for any minor offense, like simply being out past curfew or petty theft. Someone can accuse you of a crime you didn't commit and without much evidence (or any) and they're like "time to go to the death prison!" But there is a reason for this and we find out why in the second half of the book. It made sense to me, and I have to say (as vile and disgusting as it is) their reasoning did not seem outside the realm of possibility of something even our own government would do to us ... and I did appreciate Fast's overall message to fight against injustice.

I liked the romance. I didn't love it and I even have a sneaking suspicion that the author may be setting up a love triangle in the sequel, although I hope I'm wrong. It would just make the series feel even more YA than it already does. Despite my complaints this did keep my interest throughout and was pretty easy to read. I think I did like it enough to read the second one and I would recommend it if you are interested in this genre.
